Field studies of Bell’s salamander (Isthmura bellii) have provided detailed information on its early life history. Eggs deposited in cool, montane streams undergo a prolonged incubation period, with hatching occurring at approximately 50 days [ab = approximately 50 days] when maintained at 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. The newly emerged larvae are notably small; measurements indicate a wet weight at birth of just 0.0141 grams [Wwb = 0.0141 grams], a value consistent with the modest egg diameter of roughly three millimeters from which it is derived. This diminutive size at hatching reflects the lecithotrophic strategy of the endotrophic larva, which relies entirely on yolk reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. The limited initial mass of the yolk-sac larva contrasts sharply with the substantial size ultimately achieved by adult females.

In contrast to the minute neonates, adult females of Isthmura bellii attain a considerably larger body size. The ultimate wet weight for females has been recorded at 13.13 grams [Wwi = 13.13 grams], representing a nearly thousand-fold increase in mass from the hatchling stage. This substantial adult mass is characteristic of the species and contributes to its ecological role as a top invertebrate predator within its stream habitats. The pronounced growth trajectory from a 0.0141 gram larva to a 13.13 gram adult female requires a prolonged period of somatic development and resource acquisition, a pattern that is closely tied to the thermal regime of the salamander’s environment.

The pace of early development in Isthmura bellii is strongly influenced by temperature. Larval development proceeds through a series of distinct stages, culminating in metamorphosis. Under experimental conditions held at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the time since birth at metamorphosis has been recorded as approximately 92 days . This duration encompasses the period from hatching through the dramatic morphological transformation that includes gill resorption, limb development, and the transition to a terrestrial juvenile form. The rate of this larval-juvenile transition is a critical determinant of survival, as it governs the timing of the shift from an aquatic to a more terrestrial lifestyle and the associated exposure to novel predators and prey resources.

Reproductive maturity in female Isthmura bellii is not attained immediately following metamorphosis. Field and laboratory data indicate that the time since metamorphosis at puberty for females is approximately 730 days [tp = approximately 730 days] under conditions of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This extended period of juvenile growth and maturation is essential for females to accumulate the body reserves necessary to support egg production. Once mature, the species exhibits a relatively low annual reproductive output. Gravid females produce an average of 20 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 20 eggs per clutch] and are assumed to deposit approximately 3 clutches per season [F_R_i = approximately 3 clutches per season], yielding a modest annual fecundity that aligns with a slow life-history strategy typical of many high-elevation plethodontids.

The overall lifespan of Isthmura bellii is remarkably long for an amphibian of its size. Maximum longevity in the wild has been estimated at approximately 18 years [am = approximately 18 years] when individuals experience thermal conditions near 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This extended lifespan is correlated with the species’ low metabolic demands; measurements of the basal metabolic rate, recorded as a maximal oxygen consumption of 0.0033 milliliters per hour [JOi = 0.0033 milliliters per hour] at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], indicate a very low resting energy expenditure. Such a slow metabolic pace underpins the salamander’s delayed maturation, low reproductive rate, and long life, representing a classic slow life-history continuum. This energy-conserving strategy is well-suited to the cool, resource-limited environments that Isthmura bellii inhabits.
